subject: humanities
passage: Typographers have long repeated the claim that serifs, the small strokes at the ends of letters, guide the eye along a line of print and so make serif typefaces easier to read than sans serif ones. The explanation is appealing, and it fits the fact that most printed books are set in serif type. Yet studies comparing the two styles have generally found small and inconsistent differences in reading speed and comprehension, and the differences that do appear seem to depend more on a reader's familiarity with a typeface than on its serifs. The prevalence of serif type in books, then, may reflect habit and tradition at least as much as any advantage built into the letters.
stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?

choices.A: To question whether a popular explanation accounts for a common practice
choices.B: To show that familiarity is the only factor that affects how fast people read
choices.C: To argue that sans serif typefaces are easier to read than serif typefaces
choices.D: To explain how serifs guide a reader's eye along a line of printed text

explanation.why: The text presents a familiar claim (serifs make type easier to read) that seems to explain why books use serif type. "Yet" introduces studies finding "small and inconsistent differences," and the conclusion suggests the practice "may reflect habit and tradition." The author is casting doubt on the explanation, not replacing it with a strong opposite claim.
explanation.A: Correct. The author doubts that the serif-readability claim explains why books are set in serif type, suggesting habit as an alternative.
explanation.B: Incorrect. The text says differences "seem to depend more" on familiarity, a hedged comparison; "the only factor" goes far beyond it.
explanation.C: Incorrect. The studies found small, inconsistent differences, not an advantage for sans serif type; the author makes no such claim.
explanation.D: Incorrect. The text reports this explanation only to question it; it never explains how serifs would guide the eye.
